Every long-document task hides a state-tracking problem. Reading code means tracking variables as they are assigned and reassigned; following a story means tracking who holds what. The failure mode is rarely the prose — it is the bookkeeping, and it gets harder as the document gets longer.

**StateBench**, released on 3 November by the Allen Institute for AI with a tech report, dataset and code on Hugging Face, measures that bookkeeping directly. Its design choice is the interesting part: instead of testing the hardest cases only, it decomposes state tracking into four levels of *increasing* difficulty, framed as four kinds of variable assignment.

## Four Levels

- **R-trivial** — immutable assignment (`x = 4`). The model only recovers the first value; like a birth date, it never changes.
- **Aperiodic** — reassignment by value (`x = 4` then `x = 2`). Only the latest value matters; a thermostat.
- **Soluble** — self-referential updates (`x = x + 5`). Changes must be carried forward, not looked up; a running game score.
- **General finite** — assignment by reference (`x = y`, swapping two variables). The classic S₅ problem: a ball hidden under five cups, with the cups repeatedly swapped.

The hierarchy is not arbitrary — it comes from Krohn–Rhodes theory, which decomposes state-tracking problems into atomic primitives. All four benchmark variants use the same number of variables and place assignments at the same points in the sequence; only the *operation* changes.

## What It Found

On **pretrained open models** — Olmo 3 (transformer) versus Olmo Hybrid (adds Gated DeltaNet layers), plus 275M and 2.7B variants, none trained beyond 64,000 tokens — nearly all scored well on R-trivial, degraded on Aperiodic as inputs grew, and sat at chance on General finite. Format mattered: a 275M hybrid was near ceiling on RULER-style R-trivial problems but near chance on the same problems framed as spreadsheet edits.

On **frontier models** — Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Sol and Luna — the same pattern, sharper. All four handled R-trivial and Aperiodic well, then fell off a cliff on Soluble and General finite as inputs grew, dropping to **13% or less** on the longest General finite problems.

The decisive experiment was direct training. Training 275M models from scratch on up to 256 assignments and testing out to 64,000 assignments — 250x the training length — separated architecture from data. Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models generalized almost perfectly on the first three levels, with the flexible-memory Gated DeltaNet staying near-perfect out to roughly **10x** its training length. Transformers learned the easier levels and degraded on longer ones, and **never learned General finite at all**. That difference is architectural, not a data problem.

## Why It Matters

For anyone building agents that carry state over long contexts, this is a selection criterion rather than a benchmark curiosity: attention-only designs fail on exactly the dependency chains that long workflows generate, and a running recurrent memory measurably survives them. Open questions remain — the placement of limited-memory Gated DeltaNet in the hierarchy, numerical precision effects, and the fact that StateBench assumes a fixed variable count, while real conversations keep introducing new entities.
